top_choice_rationale: P001 (Helpman and Melitz, B010) rewards one identifiable discovery: firm heterogeneity produces selection into exporting, reallocation across firms and a channel for gains from trade that representative-firm new trade theory does not generate. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extends the mechanism to exporting versus foreign investment, which supports a two-name credit. The predictions have been tested on firm-level data in many countries for over twenty years, so maturity is not in doubt. The main cost is credit for precursors (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum, Hopenhayn) and for Redding's later extensions. A narrow citation on selection and reallocation, with those strands acknowledged in the scientific background, handles this reasonably, though not fully. The citation should not rest on a welfare magnitude, because the size of the gains is sensitive to distributional assumptions. My judgement rests on the mechanism, the evidence and the credit structure, not on the count of supporters, which shows only that attribution is stable across assessors. P000 is ranked last because a defensible, mature and attributable candidate is available. This assessment relies on my own recollection of the literature and is not independently verified.
recusal_note: Field proximity: my research in international trade and industrial organisation is close to the B010 topic, though I have no documented co-authorship or institutional tie to Helpman, Melitz or Redding. I co-authored a 2026 IJIO paper with the chair (Hassler) and Ellingsen, neither of whom is a candidate. My spouse's public political role is noted as a public fact only, with no apparent bearing on this ballot. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
